## Overview

This design describes reference-based multiple imputation for longitudinal
binary outcomes in `rbmi`. It uses the latent multivariate probit model in
@Cro2025 and extends the imputation step to condition on observed outcomes
after an intercurrent event (ICE), as motivated by @Rehal2026. The trial
example shows the workflow from posterior draws through imputation, analysis,
and pooling.

The design proceeds in seven sections.

1. [Example data](#example-data)
2. [Multivariate probit draw model in Stan](#sec-binary-probit)
3. [Imputation method and prototype implementation](#imputation-method-and-prototype-implementation)
4. [Firth regression](#sec-binary-firth)
5. [`rbmi` integration prototype](#rbmi-integration-prototype)
6. [Example data analysis](#example-data-analysis)
7. [Implementation plan](#sec-binary-implementation-plan)

The [companion research notes](research_binary_extension.html) cover validation
against the Cro et al. sampler, the derivation of the joint imputation correction,
sampler alternatives, and considerations for a standalone Firth implementation (which was discarded).

Rendering the examples requires the `rbmi` version from this branch, a working
CmdStan installation, and the R packages `cmdstanr`, `posterior`, `haven`,
`dplyr`, `TruncatedNormal`, and `brglm2`.

## Example data

### Case study and target estimand

@Cro2025 use an eight-week depression trial originally reported by
@Goldstein2004. The trial compared placebo, once-daily paroxetine, and two doses of
twice-daily duloxetine. Their public example combines 100 placebo patients with
100 patients randomly selected from the three non-placebo arms. Thus, the
example's active group pools treatments.

The endpoint is a reduction of more than 50% from baseline HAMD17 at Week 8,
with earlier outcomes at Weeks 1, 2, 4, and 6. Their Table 2 targets the odds of
response on active treatment relative to placebo among trial-eligible patients
with depression, using a treatment policy strategy for early treatment cessation
(regardless of whether all assigned doses were received). The paper reports that
follow-up ceased with early treatment cessation, with 70/100 active and 61/100
placebo patients completing treatment. Table 3 gives cumulative off-treatment
percentages, which coincide with missing outcome percentages in that case study.

The data used below are the high-dropout example from the
[LSHTM Missing Data website](https://www.lshtm.ac.uk/research/centres-projects-groups/missing-data#dia-missing-data), which describes these as modified demonstration data:
the active group was sampled from the non-placebo arms, and the placebo group was expanded to 100
by resampling patients, assigning new IDs, and perturbing their outcomes.

### Import the data

The code below reads `high_low_datasets.zip` beside this document, extracting
only the high-dropout dataset, `high1.sas7bdat`, into a temporary directory.
The low-dropout dataset, `low1.sas7bdat`, is not used here.

```{r}
#| label: import-antidepressant-data
#| echo: true
```

The data set contains `r nrow(antidepressant)` observed patient-visit records for
`r length(unique(antidepressant$PATIENT))` patients, and the scheduled follow-up weeks are `r knitr::combine_words(visit_weeks)`.

```{r}
head(antidepressant)
```

- `r length(unique(antidepressant$PATIENT[antidepressant$arm == "Placebo"]))` placebo
and `r length(unique(antidepressant$PATIENT[antidepressant$arm == "Active"]))`
active
- `PATIENT` identifies patients;
- `TRT` codes placebo as `1` and active as `2`;
- `week` gives scheduled follow-up week;
- `basval` is baseline HAMD17;
- `change` is follow-up minus baseline HAMD17;
- `POOLINV` identifies the pooled investigator.

Follow-up HAMD17 can be reconstructed as `basval + change`.
The derived binary `response` uses a strict >50% reduction from baseline,
as specified in Table 2:

```{r}
with(antidepressant, stopifnot(all(as.integer(change < -0.5 * basval) == response)))
```

There are no missing change scores in the
stored rows; missing follow-up assessments are represented by absent rows:

```{r}
stopifnot(!anyNA(antidepressant$change))
```

We use the full patient roster when calculating missingness at each visit.
The file has no separate treatment cessation indicator, so interpreting
missingness as off-treatment status relies on the case-study description in
@Cro2025.

### Check against Cro et al. Table 3

The comparison below counts observed change scores at each scheduled week,
uses the number of unique patients in each arm as the denominator, and compares
the resulting missing percentages with the published values.

```{r}
#| label: compare-table-3
comparison <- data.frame(Week = c(1, 2, 4, 6, 8))
for (arm in c("Placebo", "Active")) {
    n_arm <- sum(patients$arm == arm)
    observed <- vapply(comparison$Week, function(w) {
        sum(antidepressant$arm == arm & antidepressant$week == w &
            !is.na(antidepressant$change))
    }, integer(1))
    comparison[[paste(arm, "observed n")]] <- observed
    comparison[[paste(arm, "missing %")]] <- 100 * (n_arm - observed) / n_arm
}
comparison[["Placebo published %"]] <- c(0, 8, 15, 27, 39)
comparison[["Active published %"]] <- c(0, 10, 15, 25, 30)
stopifnot(
    all(comparison[["Placebo missing %"]] == comparison[["Placebo published %"]]),
    all(comparison[["Active missing %"]] == comparison[["Active published %"]])
)
knitr::kable(comparison, caption = "High-dropout data versus Cro et al. Table 3")
```

All entries in Table 3 are reproduced exactly. The missing percentages are
`r knitr::combine_words(comparison[["Placebo missing %"]])` for placebo and
`r knitr::combine_words(comparison[["Active missing %"]])` for active.
At Week 8, observed outcomes remain for
`r comparison[["Placebo observed n"]][comparison$Week == 8]`/
`r sum(patients$arm == "Placebo")` placebo patients and
`r comparison[["Active observed n"]][comparison$Week == 8]`/
`r sum(patients$arm == "Active")` active patients, matching the reported
completion counts.

### Response threshold discrepancy in the paper

Table 2 of @Cro2025 specifies a reduction of **more than 50%**, whereas the
Discussion describes **50% or more**. The published Week 8 responder counts
(25 placebo and 39 active) agree with the inclusive threshold in these data.
The following comparison makes the distinction explicit; `response` above
retains the strict threshold from Table 2.

```{r}
#| label: compare-response-thresholds
threshold_comparison <- antidepressant |>
    dplyr::filter(week == 8) |>
    dplyr::group_by(arm) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
        `Reduction >50%` = sum(response, na.rm = TRUE),
        `Reduction >=50%` = sum(-change / basval >= 0.5, na.rm = TRUE)
    ) |>
    dplyr::rename(Arm = arm) |>
    dplyr::mutate(`Published responders` = c(25L, 39L))
stopifnot(
    all(threshold_comparison[["Reduction >=50%"]] ==
        threshold_comparison[["Published responders"]])
)
knitr::kable(threshold_comparison, caption = "Week 8 responders by threshold")
```

and 2 for Active. The model and examples below use the strict response

## Multivariate probit draw model in Stan {#sec-binary-probit}

### Scope and statistical target

The draw step implements the statistical model in Section 3.3 of @Cro2025.
Preparation, posterior sampling, and parameter extraction follow the separate
operations used in `rbmi`.

To connect with Section 3.3, let a superscript $\mathrm{P}$ distinguish the
paper's latent variables and parameters from those used below. The paper indexes
arm by $t\in\{a,r\}$ where $a$ denotes active and $r$ denotes reference, and writes the model componentwise as

$$
\begin{aligned}
Z^{\mathrm{P}}_{t,i,j}&=\mu^{\mathrm{P}}_{t,j}+e^{\mathrm{P}}_{t,i,j},&
e^{\mathrm{P}}_{t,i}&\sim N_D(0,\Omega^{\mathrm{P}}_t),\\
Y_{t,i,j}&=\mathbf{1}(Z^{\mathrm{P}}_{t,i,j}\leq 0),&
\operatorname{diag}(\Omega^{\mathrm{P}}_t)&=\mathbf{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Equivalently, the subject's latent vector has distribution
$Z^{\mathrm{P}}_{t,i}\sim N_D(\mu^{\mathrm{P}}_t,\Omega^{\mathrm{P}}_t)$.
With unit diagonal $\Omega_t$ is also a correlation matrix.
Here $D$ counts the modeled binary visits: it corresponds to the paper's $J+1$
when the same visits are included. The paper includes a baseline response in
that indexing; the example here models only the five follow-up binary responses,
so $D=5$, with baseline HAMD17 available as a separate covariate.

For the implementation, index subjects across arms and let $a_i$ denote subject
$i$'s randomized arm (the paper's $t$). Conditional on the supplied design rows
$x_{ij}$, use

$$
\begin{aligned}
Z_i \mid \beta,\Omega&\sim N_D(\mu_i,\Omega_{a_i}),&
\mu_{ij}&=x_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\beta,\\
Y_{ij}&=\mathbf{1}(Z_{ij}>0),&
\operatorname{diag}(\Omega_t)&=\mathbf{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For the arm-by-visit model, the two formulations are related by the global sign change

$$
Z_{ij}=-Z^{\mathrm{P}}_{a_i,i,j},\qquad
\mu_{ij}=-\mu^{\mathrm{P}}_{a_i,j},\qquad
\Omega_t=\Omega^{\mathrm{P}}_t.
$$

The binary outcomes are unchanged (the boundary $Z=0$ has probability zero).
Thus $\Pr(Y_{ij}=1\mid\beta)=\Phi(\mu_{ij}) =\Phi(-\mu^{\mathrm{P}}_{a_i,j})$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF.
Negating every latent component preserves all covariances and correlations.

The default design has one intercept per arm and visit: $x_{ij}$ selects
coefficient $\beta_{a_i,j}$ from the vector $\beta$, which stacks one block per arm,
where
$\beta_t=(\beta_{t,1},\ldots,\beta_{t,D})^{\mathsf T}$. Consequently
$\mu_{ij}=\beta_{a_i,j}=-\mu^{\mathrm{P}}_{a_i,j}$ in this design.
Writing a single $\beta$ therefore still gives separate arm-specific means;
with the independent priors below, the default posterior factors by arm, just
as in the paper, with separate unstructured correlation matrices.
A common correlation matrix (`same_cov = TRUE`) and a supplied covariate design
are also supported. Covariates enter through $x_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\beta$;
arm-by-visit interactions allow the separate visit-specific covariate effects
described in the paper, while shared coefficients impose additional assumptions.

<!-- The default design includes no baseline covariate. A common correlation matrix
is an extension beyond the paper's separate-arm model; treatment means remain
separate when `same_cov = TRUE`. Binary observations identify correlations,
not unrestricted latent variances. -->

<!-- The supplementary code follows the paper's sign convention. Consequently compare
**Stan's $\beta$ with minus Cro's $\beta$**, after matching the design and
coefficient order, while leaving the correlation matrices unchanged. -->

The priors matching the latent model in Section 3.3 are
$p(\beta)\propto1$ and $\Omega_t\sim\operatorname{LKJ}(1)$, independently by arm.
The paper describes flat priors for that model and fixes every latent variance
to one. (Note that the Jeffreys covariance prior only occurs in Section 3.2, which instead
fits an unrestricted MVN model directly to the binary outcomes as if they were
continuous, followed by adaptive rounding.) 
To make the equivalence explicit, let
$\mathcal C_D$ be the space of positive definite $D\times D$ matrices with unit
diagonal. With density measured against the free off-diagonal entries,

$$
p(\Omega_t\mid\eta)\propto
\det(\Omega_t)^{\eta-1}\mathbf{1}(\Omega_t\in\mathcal C_D).
$$

Thus $\eta=1$ is exactly a constant density on the admissible correlation
matrices. This prior is actually proper because $\mathcal C_D$ has finite volume. 
Note that the flat mean prior remains improper.

Alternatively, iid normal priors on the regression coefficients can be used, with a standard deviation $\sigma_{\beta} > 0$. Below the corresponding parameter will be denoted by `beta_sd`.
This avoids silently using an improper posterior under separation. It is then a different prior from the paper.

### Observed-data likelihood and returned draws

Let $O_i$ be the observed visits. The fitted likelihood is the probability that
the latent signs match the observed outcomes:

$$
L_i(\beta,\Omega)=
\Pr\!\left((2Y_{ij}-1)Z_{ij}>0\text{ for all }j\in O_i
\mid\beta,\Omega\right).
$$

Missing visits are integrated out analytically before augmentation. Patients
with no observed visits contribute one and are omitted from the likelihood,
while their indices are retained in metadata. Monotone dropout is not required.
The Stan model uses the observed cells supplied to it. As in the continuous
workflow, the binary adapter uses the assigned ICE strategy to select those
cells. It retains post-ICE observations for MAR and masks them for non-MAR
strategies. The original data remain available for imputation.

The returned draws contain coefficients and latent correlation matrices only.
Once the fitting rows have been selected, Stan fits the same probit model for
each strategy. The auxiliary variables support likelihood
computation. Imputation draws fresh latent responses under the selected
reference assumption, conditional on the observed signs.

### Stan implementation and parameterization

The [Stan multivariate probit example](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/regression.html#multivariate-probit-regression)
augments the likelihood with sign-constrained normal variables. The same model
can be expressed using uniform variables and conditional normal quantiles. The
underlying transformation of multivariate normal probabilities to integrals over
the unit cube is described by @Genz1992. For multivariate probit specifically,
@Goodrich2016 implemented this parameterization in Stan's `probit-multi-good.stan`
example. His [accompanying explanation](https://groups.google.com/g/stan-users/c/G3HAQ3dp1f8)
describes the sequential quantile transformation and its Jacobian adjustment,
also motivated by low BFMI in the sign-constrained formulation. A published
extension to dichotomous and ordinal diagnostic tests builds on Goodrich's code
[@Cerullo2022, Section 3.5 and Supplementary Material 5].

We use this equivalent parameterization below because the direct sign-constrained
version had low E-BFMI and divergences in an initial fit to this example. With the
change-of-variables adjustment included, it preserves the marginal posterior for
$\beta$ and $\Omega$.

For the observed subvector of a patient, let $L L^{\mathsf T}=\Omega[O_i,O_i]$,
where $O_i = \{j: Y_{ij} \text{ is observed}\}$, as well as
$s_j=2Y_{ij}-1$, $Z=\mu+Le$, and

$$
c_j=\mu_j+\sum_{k<j}L_{jk}e_k,\quad
p_j=\Phi(s_jc_j/L_{jj}),\quad
u_j\in(0,1),\quad e_j=-s_j\Phi^{-1}(u_jp_j).
$$

The change of variables from sign-constrained $Z$ to $u$ has Jacobian that
cancels the conditional normal density except for $p_j$. Hence the augmented
target contributes $\sum_j\log p_j$, with independent uniform base measures for
$u$. Integrating out $u$ recovers the likelihood above. We implement
$u_j=\Phi(v_j)$ with $v_j\sim N(0,1)$ for unconstrained auxiliary parameters.
These variables are parameters sampled jointly with $\beta$ and $\Omega$, not newly simulated
numbers inserted into an approximate likelihood. The final uniform for each
subject has no effect on the weight and is integrated out, leaving
$\sum_i(|O_i|-1)$ auxiliary parameters. A one-visit patient needs none. The internal
calculation uses reverse visit order; this changes sampling efficiency, not the
joint likelihood or the visit labels in the returned matrices.

Patients sharing an observed-visit pattern and a covariance group share a matrix
factorization. We factor the principal submatrix of $\Omega$; simply taking
the corresponding rows and columns of its full Cholesky factor would generally
be wrong. Probabilities are computed using `normal_lcdf`, without probability
clipping or `Phi_approx`. The helper computes normal quantiles from log
probabilities: it uses symmetry
and, in the far tail, six Newton updates of the log-CDF equation. This avoids
exponentiating extremely small probabilities or subtracting them from one.
Invalid proposals at floating-point singularities are still rejected by Stan.
This is a prototype for
moderate-dimensional longitudinal data, not a claim of robust sampling for
arbitrary rare outcomes, separation, or nearly singular correlations.

```{r}
#| label: probit-stan-source
#| echo: true
```

For this strongly correlated example, the fit helper first adapts the NUTS metric,
then starts sampling from each chain's final state with the learned metric and a
step size no larger than 0.005. The adaptation-stage iteration is discarded.
This conservative cap costs runtime but addresses divergences that remained with
ordinary step-size adaptation. It is a tuning choice, not a modification of the
model. Final diagnostics still need to be checked on every new dataset. `cmdstanr`
is used here for convenient standalone compilation; integration with the package's
existing `rstan` infrastructure is deferred.

### Validation summary

In the recorded trial comparison, the posterior means of all 30 coefficients
and correlations agreed with the corrected reference sampler within 2.09
combined Monte Carlo standard errors. The Stan chains had no divergences or
maximum-treedepth hits. The [research notes](research_binary_extension.html#sec-binary-probit-validation)
give the reference implementation, reproduction instructions, independent
checks and performance considerations.

## Imputation method and prototype implementation

The imputation step uses the fitted parameters to construct a latent
distribution under a reference assumption. Then it conditions on all observed
responses, including outcomes measured after treatment discontinuation.

### Means and hybrid covariance definition {#sec-binary-reference-distribution}

For one joint posterior draw of $\beta$ and the arm-specific correlation
matrices, write $\mu_{t,ij}=x_{t,ij}^{\mathsf T}\beta$ for patient $i$'s latent
mean at visit $j$ under arm $t\in\{a,r\}$. Here $x_{t,ij}$ uses the patient's
baseline covariates with the arm set to $t$. We retain the implementation's
convention $Y_{ij}=\mathbf{1}(Z_{ij}>0)$, which reverses the latent means in
@Cro2025 but leaves covariances unchanged.

Let $d_i$ be the last scheduled visit before treatment discontinuation, with
$P_i=\{1,\ldots,d_i\}$ and $Q_i=\{d_i+1,\ldots,D\}$. These are treatment-status
blocks, not observed/missing blocks: a visit in either block may be missing,
and visits in $Q_i$ may be observed. For an active-arm patient the full latent
mean vector is defined componentwise as follows, following Section 3.2.1 of
@Cro2025:

| Assumption | $j\leq d_i$ | $j>d_i$ |
|:-----------|:------------|:---------|
| MAR | $\mu_{a,ij}$ | $\mu_{a,ij}$ |
| JR (J2R) | $\mu_{a,ij}$ | $\mu_{r,ij}$ |
| LMCF | $\mu_{a,ij}$ | $\mu_{a,i d_i}$ |
| CIR | $\mu_{a,ij}$ | $\mu_{a,i d_i}+\mu_{r,ij}-\mu_{r,i d_i}$ |
| CR | $\mu_{r,ij}$ | $\mu_{r,ij}$ |

These means apply to observed as well as missing visits when constructing the
joint distribution; observed binary values are preserved by conditioning on
their signs. In particular, CR changes the pre-discontinuation means too.
CIR and LMCF operate on the latent mean scale, not directly on response
probabilities. For a reference-arm patient, MAR/J2R/CIR/CR all use $\mu_{r,ij}$;
LMCF carries forward $\mu_{r,i d_i}$ after discontinuation if assigned to that arm.

For the covariance, partition the posterior arm matrices $A=\Omega_a$ and
$R=\Omega_r$ by $P_i,Q_i$, suppressing the patient index on the blocks. Define

$$
B=R_{QP}R_{PP}^{-1},\qquad
V=R_{QQ}-R_{QP}R_{PP}^{-1}R_{PQ}.
$$

For an active-arm patient under J2R, CIR, or CR, the hybrid covariance specified
in @Cro2025 is

$$
\Sigma_i^{\mathrm{ref}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
A_{PP} & A_{PP}B^{\mathsf T}\\
BA_{PP} & V+BA_{PP}B^{\mathsf T}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

It preserves the active pre-discontinuation covariance and the reference
conditional regression $B$ and residual covariance $V$. Equivalently,
$Z_Q\mid Z_P\sim N(\mu_Q^{\mathrm{ref}}+
B(Z_P-\mu_P^{\mathrm{ref}}),V)$. This construction is positive definite when
$A$ and $R$ are positive definite. In particular, Cro's CR covariance uses this
same hybrid, rather than replacing the entire covariance with $R$.
MAR and LMCF retain the patient's randomized-arm covariance; reference-arm
patients retain $R$ under all five assumptions.

Although $A$ and $R$ have unit diagonals, the hybrid post-discontinuation block
need not: it equals $R_{QQ}+B(A_{PP}-R_{PP})B^{\mathsf T}$. With only one
pre-discontinuation visit, $A_{PP}=R_{PP}=1$, so its diagonal is still one.
With multiple pre-discontinuation visits, the arm correlation blocks can
differ. Use the constructed diagonal when sampling. A common fitted covariance
also makes the hybrid equal to that common covariance.

For $d_i=D$ there is no post-discontinuation block and the ordinary randomized-arm
model is used. When the ICE affects the first scheduled visit ($d_i=0$), JR,
CR, and CIR use the reference distribution throughout, matching continuous
`rbmi` at this boundary. MAR retains the randomized-arm distribution. LMCF
requires a scheduled pre-ICE visit whose modeled mean can be carried forward.
That visit's outcome may be missing. The joint sampler conditions on the
observed signs at any visits, including when the first outcome is missing.

### Corrected imputation algorithm {#sec-binary-joint-sampling}

A patient's observed responses constrain the signs of the corresponding
latent variables. The [research notes](research_binary_extension.html#sec-binary-original-imputation)
derive why imposing each sign in a single forward pass can change the
imputation distribution. To generate each completed dataset:

1. Take one joint posterior draw of the coefficients and covariance matrices,
   shared across patients, and construct each patient's full
   $(\mu_i^{\mathrm{ref}},\Sigma_i^{\mathrm{ref}})$ as defined in @sec-binary-reference-distribution.
2. Draw the **entire latent vector jointly** from that multivariate normal,
   subject to the coordinate bounds
   $$
   (\ell_{ij},u_{ij})=
   \begin{cases}
   (0,\infty),&Y_{ij}=1,\\
   (-\infty,0),&Y_{ij}=0,\\
   (-\infty,\infty),&Y_{ij}\text{ missing}.
   \end{cases}
   $$
   Thus all observed signs, including later and post-discontinuation signs,
   constrain the same joint draw. No first-visit observation is required.
3. Replace only missing binary outcomes by $\mathbf{1}(Z_{ij}>0)$, retaining all
   observed values. Repeat with further posterior draws for further imputations.

For computation, joint sampling can alternatively be factored into a truncated
MVN draw for the observed coordinates and an ordinary conditional Gaussian draw
for the missing coordinates. This is exactly equivalent and can reduce the
truncated sampling dimension when many visits are missing. Patients without
observed outcomes need only an ordinary MVN draw; complete patients need no
imputation.

The prototype uses `TruncatedNormal::rtmvnorm()` [@Botev2017] for the joint
draw. See the [sampler comparison](research_binary_extension.html#sec-binary-sampler-choice).

Observed post-discontinuation responses can inform missing outcomes for the
same patient through this conditioning step. Learning off-treatment means
across patients also uses those responses in the draw model.

### Off-treatment modelling {#sec-binary-off-treatment}

The count draw model retains all observed positive-duration counts, including
off-treatment counts, regardless of the assigned imputation strategy. The
longitudinal data object sets the count fit mask to `TRUE` throughout, and
`prepare_stan_data_count()` selects observed cells with positive duration.
The count imputer builds its predictor rows from the same formula used for
fitting. Each row keeps its covariate values when the arm is changed for a
reference prediction. [R/longData.R](../R/longData.R) · [R/mcmc_count.R](../R/mcmc_count.R) · [R/impute_count.R](../R/impute_count.R)

For binary outcomes, use the continuous fitting rule and the count model's
row-level covariate approach. In a retrieved-dropout analysis, assign MAR and
include a visit-level `off_treatment` covariate [@Rehal2026]. The retrieved
responses can then inform a common shift on the latent scale. With a non-MAR
strategy, observed responses from the first affected visit onward are masked
for that subject, as in a Cro-style reference-based analysis. In a mixed
strategy analysis, only subjects whose post-ICE observations enter the fit
contribute data on off-treatment response.

Supply treatment status for every scheduled visit, including those with
missing outcomes. Where a recorded ICE marks treatment discontinuation,
its first affected visit can define the indicator. MAR uses the fitted mean
at the patient's actual arm and status, then conditions on the original
observations with the same joint sampler and latent correlation model. See
the [small off-treatment example](#small-example-with-off-treatment-modelling).

### Prototype and example

This prototype uses the saturated arm-by-visit model above, with placebo as
reference and copy increments in reference (CIR) for active patients. The
last observed visit serves as the last on-treatment visit because no cessation
dates are supplied. Intermittent gaps therefore fall in the on-treatment
block.

First obtain 500 paired draws of the coefficients and correlation matrices.
If both saved files are available, the example checks that the inputs match
before reusing the recorded trial fit. If either file is absent, it fits the
trial model in Stan. The imputer samples fresh latent responses for each
completed dataset.

```{r}
#| label: cir-posterior-draws
n_imp <- 500L
probit_input <- prepare_probit_data(Ycat, treat1, same_cov = FALSE)
saved_fit <- file.path(dirname(archive), "rbmi-binary-prototype", "stan_release.rds")
saved_data <- file.path(dirname(saved_fit), "data.rds")
if (file.exists(saved_fit) && file.exists(saved_data)) {
    saved_input <- readRDS(saved_data)
    stopifnot(identical(Ycat, saved_input$Y), identical(treat1, saved_input$arm))
    saved <- readRDS(saved_fit)
    probit_fit <- list(
        prepared = probit_input,
        fit = list(draws = function(variables) {
            posterior::subset_draws(saved$draws, variable = variables)
        }),
        diagnostics = saved$diagnostics
    )
} else {
    probit_model <- cmdstanr::cmdstan_model(cmdstanr::write_stan_file(probit_stan_code))
    probit_fit <- fit_probit_draws(probit_input, probit_model, init = 0)
    print(probit_fit$fit$diagnostic_summary())
}
cir_parameters <- extract_probit_draws(probit_fit, n_samples = n_imp, seed = 20261102)
```

The helper below implements the corrected full-vector sampler using
[`TruncatedNormal::rtmvnorm`](https://lbelzile.github.io/TruncatedNormal/reference/rtmvnorm.html).
It takes the last on-treatment visit from `last_on` and conditions on the
observed responses at any visit. This standalone CIR helper assumes at least
one scheduled pre-ICE visit. The general sampler also handles an ICE at the
first scheduled visit. Sampler warnings stop execution.

```{r}
#| label: cir-imputation-function
#| time_it: true
binary_references <- function(references, arm, has_non_mar) {
    if (is.null(references)) {
        if (has_non_mar) {
            stop("Please specify `references` for non-MAR imputation.", call. = FALSE)
        }
        references <- setNames(levels(arm), levels(arm))
    }
    rbmi:::validate(rbmi:::add_class(references, "references"), arm)
    if (!all(levels(arm) %in% names(references))) {
        stop("`references` must provide a mapping for every treatment group.", call. = FALSE)
    }
    references
}

impute_cir <- function(Y, arm, last_on, parameters, references, seed = 20261103) {
    D <- ncol(Y)
    arm_levels <- parameters$metadata$arm_levels
    arm <- match(as.character(arm), arm_levels)
    reference_arm <- match(unname(references[arm_levels]), arm_levels)[arm]
    stopifnot(
        length(arm) == nrow(Y), !anyNA(arm), !anyNA(reference_arm),
        length(last_on) == nrow(Y), all(last_on %in% seq_len(D)),
        all(Y[!is.na(Y)] %in% 0:1),
        length(arm_levels) == 2L,
        !parameters$metadata$same_cov,
        length(parameters$beta[[1]]) == 2L * D
    )
    set.seed(seed)
    incomplete <- which(rowSums(is.na(Y)) > 0L)
    lapply(seq_along(parameters$beta), function(m) {
        # Each completed dataset shares ONE joint parameter draw across patients.
        means <- matrix(parameters$beta[[m]], nrow = D, ncol = 2)
        completed <- Y
        for (i in incomplete) {
            mu <- means[, arm[i]]
            Sigma <- parameters$sigma[[m]][[arm[i]]]
            d <- last_on[i]
            ref <- reference_arm[i]
            if (ref != arm[i] && d < D) {
                A <- Sigma
                R <- parameters$sigma[[m]][[ref]]
                pre <- seq_len(d)
                post <- seq.int(d + 1L, D)
                # Here we use the copy increments approach to adjust the mean vector
                # for the post-discontinuation visits based on the last observed visit.
                mu[post] <- means[d, arm[i]] + means[post, ref] - means[d, ref]
                # Compute the conditional covariance for the post-discontinuation visits.
                B <- R[post, pre, drop = FALSE] %*% solve(R[pre, pre, drop = FALSE])
                V <- R[post, post, drop = FALSE] - B %*% R[pre, post, drop = FALSE]
                cross <- B %*% A[pre, pre, drop = FALSE]
                Sigma[post, pre] <- cross
                Sigma[pre, post] <- t(cross)
                Sigma[post, post] <- V + cross %*% t(B)
            }
            Sigma <- (Sigma + t(Sigma)) / 2 # Remove floating-point asymmetry only.
            y <- Y[i, ]
            # Joint truncated multivariate normal sampling of the latent variables
            # corresponding to the observed binary responses.
            lower <- rep(-Inf, D)
            upper <- rep(Inf, D)
            lower[which(y == 1)] <- 0
            upper[which(y == 0)] <- 0
            z <- withCallingHandlers(
                as.numeric(TruncatedNormal::rtmvnorm(
                    n = 1, mu = mu, sigma = Sigma, lb = lower, ub = upper
                )),
                warning = function(w) stop(conditionMessage(w), call. = FALSE)
            )
            stopifnot(length(z) == D, all(is.finite(z)), all(z >= lower & z <= upper))
            # Impute the missing binary responses based on the sampled latent variables.
            missing <- is.na(y)
            completed[i, missing] <- as.integer(z[missing] > 0)
        }
        completed
    })
}

last_on <- apply(Ycat, 1, function(y) max(which(!is.na(y))))
cir_references <- c("1" = "1", "2" = "1")
cir_completed <- impute_cir(Ycat, treat1, last_on, cir_parameters, cir_references)

stopifnot(
    length(cir_completed) == n_imp,
    all(vapply(cir_completed, function(y) {
        !anyNA(y) && all(y %in% 0:1) &&
            all(y[!is.na(Ycat)] == Ycat[!is.na(Ycat)])
    }, logical(1)))
)
```

`cir_completed` is a list of `r length(cir_completed)` completed
`r nrow(Ycat)`-by-`r ncol(Ycat)` response matrices, with
patient IDs and visit names retained. Every observed response was preserved
and every missing response was filled. This step took
`r runtime_seconds("cir-imputation-function")` seconds using
`TruncatedNormal` `r as.character(utils::packageVersion("TruncatedNormal"))`.

#### Reusing covariance and missingness calculations

`impute_binary_fast()` extends the CIR sampler to all five strategies. Within each
posterior draw, it computes and checks the covariance once per arm, strategy,
and ICE time. The mean is evaluated for each patient with missing outcomes
using that patient’s covariates under both the randomized and reference arms.
Bounds and missing indices are prepared once per observed response pattern,
including the observed signs.
Covariances must still be recomputed for each new posterior draw; missingness
alone does not determine them. Patient order and the individual sampler calls
are unchanged, allowing an exact comparison with the same seed.

```{r}
#| label: cir-fast-function
binary_strategy <- function(strategy) {
    stopifnot(is.character(strategy), !anyNA(strategy))
    strategy[strategy == "J2R"] <- "JR"
    if (!all(strategy %in% c("MAR", "JR", "CR", "CIR", "LMCF"))) {
        stop("Binary strategies are MAR, JR (J2R), CR, CIR, and LMCF.", call. = FALSE)
    }
    strategy
}

binary_mean <- function(means, arm, ref, d, strategy) {
    D <- nrow(means)
    mu <- means[, arm]
    if (strategy == "MAR" || d == D) {
        return(mu)
    }

    post <- seq.int(d + 1L, D)
    if (strategy == "LMCF") {
        mu[post] <- means[d, arm]
        return(mu)
    }
    if (ref == arm) {
        return(mu)
    }
    if (d == 0L || strategy == "CR") {
        return(means[, ref])
    }

    mu[post] <- if (strategy == "JR") {
        means[post, ref]
    } else {
        means[d, arm] + means[post, ref] - means[d, ref]
    }
    mu
}

binary_covariance <- function(covariances, arm, ref, d, strategy) {
    if (length(covariances) == 1L) {
        return(covariances[[1L]])
    }
    Sigma <- covariances[[arm]]
    D <- nrow(Sigma)
    if (strategy %in% c("MAR", "LMCF") || d == D || ref == arm) {
        return(Sigma)
    }

    R <- covariances[[ref]]
    if (d == 0L) {
        return(R)
    }
    post <- seq.int(d + 1L, D)
    pre <- seq_len(d)
    B <- R[post, pre, drop = FALSE] %*% solve(R[pre, pre, drop = FALSE])
    V <- R[post, post, drop = FALSE] - B %*% R[pre, post, drop = FALSE]
    cross <- B %*% Sigma[pre, pre, drop = FALSE]
    Sigma[post, pre] <- cross
    Sigma[pre, post] <- t(cross)
    Sigma[post, post] <- V + cross %*% t(B)
    (Sigma + t(Sigma)) / 2
}

binary_distribution <- function(means, covariances, arm, ref, d, strategy) {
    list(
        mu = binary_mean(means, arm, ref, d, strategy),
        Sigma = binary_covariance(covariances, arm, ref, d, strategy)
    )
}

impute_binary_fast <- function(
  Y, arm, last_on, parameters, references, strategy, seed = NULL,
  baseline = NULL, visit_covariates = NULL
) {
    N <- nrow(Y)
    D <- ncol(Y)
    if (is.null(baseline)) baseline <- matrix(numeric(), N, 0L)
    Q <- ncol(baseline)
    V <- if (is.null(visit_covariates)) 0L else dim(visit_covariates)[3L]
    intercept_idx <- seq_len(2L * D)
    baseline_idx <- 2L * D + seq_len(Q * D)
    visit_idx <- (2L + Q) * D + seq_len(V)
    arm_levels <- parameters$metadata$arm_levels
    arm <- match(as.character(arm), arm_levels)
    reference_arm <- match(unname(references[arm_levels]), arm_levels)[arm]
    strategy <- binary_strategy(strategy)
    stopifnot(
        length(arm) == nrow(Y), !anyNA(arm), !anyNA(reference_arm),
        length(strategy) == nrow(Y),
        length(last_on) == nrow(Y), all(last_on %in% 0:D),
        all(Y[!is.na(Y)] %in% 0:1),
        length(arm_levels) == 2L,
        nrow(baseline) == N,
        is.null(visit_covariates) || identical(dim(visit_covariates)[1:2], c(N, D)),
        length(parameters$beta[[1]]) == (2L + Q) * D + V
    )
    if (any(strategy == "LMCF" & last_on == 0L)) {
        stop("LMCF requires a scheduled visit before the ICE.", call. = FALSE)
    }
    if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)
    incomplete <- which(rowSums(is.na(Y)) > 0L)

    # Use a common cache entry whenever the distribution reduces to MAR.
    effective_strategy <- strategy
    effective_strategy[last_on == D | (arm == reference_arm & strategy != "LMCF")] <- "MAR"
    effective_last_on <- ifelse(effective_strategy == "MAR", D, last_on)
    baseline <- baseline[incomplete, , drop = FALSE]
    if (V > 0L) {
        visit_covariates <- matrix(visit_covariates[incomplete, , , drop = FALSE],
            nrow = length(incomplete) * D, ncol = V
        )
    }
    group_key <- paste(arm[incomplete], effective_strategy[incomplete],
        effective_last_on[incomplete],
        sep = ":"
    )
    group <- match(group_key, unique(group_key))
    representatives <- incomplete[!duplicated(group_key)]
    pattern_key <- apply(Y[incomplete, , drop = FALSE], 1, paste, collapse = ":")
    pattern <- match(pattern_key, unique(pattern_key))
    bounds <- lapply(incomplete[!duplicated(pattern_key)], function(i) {
        y <- Y[i, ]
        lower <- rep(-Inf, D)
        upper <- rep(Inf, D)
        lower[which(y == 1)] <- 0
        upper[which(y == 0)] <- 0
        list(lower = lower, upper = upper, missing = which(is.na(y)))
    })

    lapply(seq_along(parameters$beta), function(m) {
        beta <- parameters$beta[[m]]
        means <- matrix(beta[intercept_idx], nrow = D, ncol = 2)
        contributions <- baseline %*% matrix(beta[baseline_idx], nrow = Q, ncol = D)
        if (V > 0L) {
            contributions <- contributions + matrix(visit_covariates %*% beta[visit_idx],
                nrow = length(incomplete), ncol = D
            )
        }
        covariances <- lapply(representatives, function(i) {
            Sigma <- binary_covariance(
                parameters$sigma[[m]], arm[i], reference_arm[i],
                effective_last_on[i], effective_strategy[i]
            )
            # These are rtmvnorm's covariance checks, done once per group.
            stopifnot(
                isSymmetric(Sigma), all(diag(Sigma) > 0),
                all(eigen(Sigma, only.values = TRUE)$values > 0)
            )
            Sigma
        })
        completed <- Y
        for (k in seq_along(incomplete)) {
            i <- incomplete[k]
            patient_means <- means + contributions[k, ]
            mu <- binary_mean(
                patient_means, arm[i], reference_arm[i], effective_last_on[i], effective_strategy[i]
            )
            b <- bounds[[pattern[k]]]
            z <- withCallingHandlers(
                as.numeric(TruncatedNormal::rtmvnorm(
                    n = 1, mu = mu, sigma = covariances[[group[k]]],
                    lb = b$lower, ub = b$upper, check = FALSE
                )),
                warning = function(w) stop(conditionMessage(w), call. = FALSE)
            )
            stopifnot(length(z) == D, all(is.finite(z)), all(z >= b$lower & z <= b$upper))
            completed[i, b$missing] <- as.integer(z[b$missing] > 0)
        }
        completed
    })
}
```

The following comparison times both implementations on the same posterior draws
and checks exact equality of all completed datasets and the final RNG state.
The sampler still performs its own tilting setup for each patient; this version
uses the public package API and avoids copying package internals.

```{r}
#| label: cir-speed-comparison
cir_time_original <- system.time(
    cir_original_check <- impute_cir(Ycat, treat1, last_on, cir_parameters, cir_references)
)[["elapsed"]]
cir_rng_original <- .Random.seed
cir_time_fast <- system.time(
    cir_completed_fast <- impute_binary_fast(
        Ycat, treat1, last_on, cir_parameters, cir_references, rep("CIR", nrow(Ycat)),
        seed = 20261103L
    )
)[["elapsed"]]
stopifnot(
    identical(cir_original_check, cir_completed_fast),
    identical(cir_rng_original, .Random.seed),
    identical(cir_completed, cir_completed_fast)
)
```

For `r length(cir_completed_fast)` imputations, the original took
`r sprintf("%.2f", cir_time_original)` seconds and the cached version took
`r sprintf("%.2f", cir_time_fast)` seconds
(a `r sprintf("%.2f", cir_time_original / cir_time_fast)`-fold speedup).
All completed datasets and the final RNG states were identical.

## Firth regression {#sec-binary-firth}

Multiple imputation fits the endpoint model to every completed dataset. With
sparse responses, even one imputation with complete or quasi-complete
separation can interrupt the analysis. For example, if nobody responds in one
arm and some patients respond in the other, the ordinary logistic likelihood
has no finite treatment coefficient. A numerical fit may return a large
coefficient and standard error even if it reports convergence.

Firth logistic regression reduces first-order coefficient bias by maximizing
the log-likelihood $\ell(\beta)$ with a Jeffreys penalty, i.e. $\ell(\beta) +
\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det I(\beta)$, where $I$ is the expected information. It gives
finite estimates under separation for a full-rank logistic design. Both
randomized arms must still be represented to estimate the treatment contrast.
If Firth is selected, we apply it to every completed dataset so the estimates
and standard errors entering Rubin's rules come from the same analysis method.
See [Firth (1993)](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/80.1.27) and
[Kosmidis and Firth (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/asaa052).

The prototype uses `brglm2` as an optional dependency. The analysis callback
`binary_logistic()` defaults to maximum likelihood. With `method = "firth"`,
it uses `brglm2::brglmFit` through `glm()` for mean bias reduction and returns
the treatment coefficient, standard error and residual degrees of freedom for
Rubin pooling. The endpoint callback fits an unadjusted two-arm logistic model.
The [research notes](research_binary_extension.html#sec-binary-firth-research) compare
the implementation options and give the adjusted-score algorithm and
unadjusted closed form.

## `rbmi` integration prototype

The proposed entry point is `draws(..., outcome = "binary")`, following the
branch's `draws()` spelling and endpoint selector. Use one row per subject and
scheduled visit, including rows with missing outcomes. Visit factor levels
give chronological order.
`data_ice` gives the **first affected visit** and strategy for each subject
with a recorded ICE. Subjects without an ICE use MAR. The prototype supports
all five built-in strategies described in @sec-binary-reference-distribution.
`JR` is the public `rbmi` name for Jump to Reference, and `J2R` is accepted
as an alias. Custom strategies and delta adjustments are outside this prototype.

| Strategy | Latent means | Latent covariance |
|:---------|:-------------|:------------------|
| MAR | Randomized arm throughout | Randomized arm |
| JR (J2R) | Randomized arm before the ICE, reference arm from the ICE | Hybrid |
| CR | Reference arm throughout | Hybrid |
| CIR | Randomized arm before the ICE, reference increments from the last pre-ICE randomized-arm mean | Hybrid |
| LMCF | Randomized arm before the ICE, last pre-ICE randomized-arm mean carried forward | Randomized arm |

For the hybrid, the binary prototype retains the randomized-arm pre-ICE
covariance and uses the reference-arm conditional regression and residual
covariance after the ICE. Continuous `rbmi` CR instead uses the full reference
covariance, so observed pre-ICE responses can inform binary CR predictions
differently. When the first scheduled visit is affected, JR, CR, and CIR use
the full reference distribution and LMCF is unavailable. A missing first
outcome alone does not constrain strategy choice.

Supply a named character vector `references` for non-MAR strategies, with one
entry per randomized arm. Mapping an arm to itself reduces JR, CR, and CIR to
that arm's distribution. LMCF uses the randomized-arm parameters for any
mapping. For MAR-only imputation, the default maps each arm to itself.

The local functions implement the four steps with column names supplied
through `set_vars()`. The Bayesian model supports two arms, arm-by-visit
intercepts, optional baseline and visit-level covariates, and shared or
arm-specific unstructured latent correlations. It uses the Stan model and
sampler in @sec-binary-probit. Package integration would add binary dispatch
to `draws()` and `impute()`, expose sampler controls, and let `analyse()`
recognize the binary imputation class. Rubin pooling already accepts the
analysis result.

### Draw and impute

Use `set_vars(covariates = ...)` to name complete numeric or categorical
columns. The prototype uses standard R model-matrix coding for additive
predictors. Model-matrix columns that are constant within subject have
visit-specific slopes. Columns that vary within subject have one slope
across visits. Both sets of slopes are shared across arms. Under a reference
arm, the arm-by-visit intercepts change and the patient's recorded covariate
values stay fixed. The draw object retains these design inputs so that
fitting and imputation use the same coding.

As in continuous `rbmi`, retain observed post-ICE responses in the fit for
MAR and mask them from the first affected visit onward for non-MAR strategies.
Imputation conditions on the original observations for every strategy.

Use `binary_impute(update_strategy = ...)` with subject ID and strategy columns
named by `vars` to change the strategy for an existing ICE. Reuse the fit
when the same observed outcomes would enter it. This includes changes
between non-MAR strategies and switches to or from MAR when every affected
response is missing. A switch that changes which observed responses enter
the fit requires a refit. Changing the reference mapping reuses the fit.
Adding, removing, or moving an ICE requires preparing the draw data again.
An optional fitted model can be reused when its prepared inputs match.

`method_bayes_binary()` is a prototype wrapper around `rbmi::method_bayes()`
that adds `prior_beta_sd`. The default of zero uses flat priors and requires
both outcomes in every arm-by-visit cell after ICE masking. With covariates,
a positive `prior_beta_sd` is required. This gives each latent probit coefficient
an independent `Normal(0, prior_beta_sd^2)` prior. At zero-valued design
covariates, the arm-by-visit intercept prior centers the response
probability at 0.5. Covariate scale determines the prior scale
of a change in prediction, so center and scale continuous inputs as appropriate.
In a cell with only one observed outcome category, both the prior and
likelihood inform the mean. In an entirely unobserved cell, the likelihood
contains no term for its intercept, so the intercept posterior is its prior.
With covariates, the shared visit slopes can still learn from the other arm.
For MAR imputation in that cell, observed responses at other visits can still inform a
patient's prediction through the latent correlation model. Firth adjustment
acts later, in the completed-data logistic regression.

Binary fitting supports `covariance = "us"`. With `same_cov = TRUE`, both
arms share one latent correlation matrix and retain separate means. The
hybrid for JR, CR, and CIR reduces to that shared matrix. With
`same_cov = FALSE`, the sampler estimates a matrix for each arm. Both
`prior_cov = "default"` and `"lkj"` resolve to LKJ(1) for binary.

New fits use `control_bayes()` fields `warmup`, `thin`, `chains`, `seed` and
`init`. Initialization accepts `"auto"` (zero), `"random"` (Stan radius 2),
or a nonnegative Stan initialization radius. Optional binary controls
`iter_sampling` (default 2000 raw iterations per chain) and `parallel_chains`
(default `chains`) can be supplied through `control_bayes(...)`. Other
control fields are rejected. `n_samples` is the number of paired draws
selected without replacement across the retained chains. The adapter checks
the requested count against the sampling budget before compiling or sampling.

The draw object retains the CmdStan sampling and warmup fits, diagnostics, and
the initial values used to start sampling. With a supplied fit, the adapter
uses its existing draws and diagnostics, checks its prepared data, and
ignores the requested fitting controls except for the seed used to select
draws. The optional `binary_draws(seed = ...)` overrides the control seed.
For imputation, `binary_impute(seed = NULL)` consumes the current R random
stream, as in continuous and count imputation. Pass an explicit seed to
repeat imputations or pair random draws across strategy runs.

```{r}
#| label: binary-integration-draws
method_bayes_binary <- function(
  same_cov = TRUE, n_samples = 20L, prior_beta_sd = 0,
  control = rbmi::control_bayes(warmup = 1500L, thin = 1L, chains = 4L)
) {
    method <- rbmi::method_bayes(
        covariance = "us", same_cov = same_cov, n_samples = n_samples,
        prior_cov = "lkj", control = control
    )
    method$prior_beta_sd <- prior_beta_sd
    method
}

binary_fit_control <- function(control, seed) {
    supported <- c("warmup", "thin", "chains", "init", "seed", "iter_sampling", "parallel_chains")
    unsupported <- setdiff(names(control), supported)
    if (length(unsupported)) {
        stop("Unsupported binary fitting controls: ", paste(unsupported, collapse = ", "),
            call. = FALSE
        )
    }
    init <- control$init
    if (identical(init, "auto")) init <- 0
    if (identical(init, "random")) init <- 2
    settings <- list(
        chains = control$chains,
        parallel_chains = control$parallel_chains %||% control$chains,
        iter_warmup = control$warmup,
        iter_sampling = control$iter_sampling %||% 2000L,
        thin = control$thin,
        seed = seed
    )
    for (name in names(settings)) binary_positive_integer(settings[[name]], name)
    stopifnot(
        settings$parallel_chains <= settings$chains,
        is.numeric(init), length(init) == 1L, is.finite(init), init >= 0
    )
    c(settings, list(init = init))
}

binary_positive_integer <- function(value, name) {
    if (!is.numeric(value) || length(value) != 1L || !is.finite(value) ||
        value < 1 || value > .Machine$integer.max || value != floor(value)) {
        stop("`", name, "` must be a positive integer.", call. = FALSE)
    }
}

# Arm-by-visit intercepts, visit-specific baseline slopes and common visit-covariate slopes.
binary_design <- function(Y, arm, baseline = NULL, visit_covariates = NULL) {
    N <- nrow(Y)
    D <- ncol(Y)
    if (is.null(baseline)) baseline <- matrix(numeric(), N, 0L)
    Q <- ncol(baseline)
    A <- nlevels(arm)
    V <- if (is.null(visit_covariates)) 0L else dim(visit_covariates)[3L]
    X <- array(0, c(N, D, (A + Q) * D + V))
    dimnames(X) <- list(NULL, NULL, c(
        as.vector(outer(colnames(Y), levels(arm), function(v, a) paste(a, v, sep = ":"))),
        if (Q > 0L) as.vector(outer(colnames(baseline), colnames(Y), paste, sep = ":")),
        dimnames(visit_covariates)[[3L]]
    ))
    for (d in seq_len(D)) {
        X[cbind(seq_len(N), d, (as.integer(arm) - 1L) * D + d)] <- 1
        if (Q > 0L) X[, d, A * D + (d - 1L) * Q + seq_len(Q)] <- baseline
    }
    if (V > 0L) X[, , (A + Q) * D + seq_len(V)] <- visit_covariates
    X
}

binary_fit_mask <- function(Y, last_on, strategy) {
    !is.na(Y) & col(Y) > last_on & strategy != "MAR"
}

# Binary counterpart of rbmi::draws() and its draws.bayes() method.
#
# data: Long data with one row per subject and visit and a 0/1/NA outcome.
# data_ice: Optional subject, first affected visit and strategy columns.
# vars: Column mapping from rbmi::set_vars() including optional covariates.
# method: method_bayes_binary() or rbmi::method_bayes() with unstructured correlations.
# outcome: Endpoint selector, "binary" for this prototype.
# fit: Optional Stan fit for the same prepared data.
# seed: Optional override for the method control seed.
binary_draws <- function(
  data,
  data_ice = NULL,
  vars,
  method,
  outcome = "binary",
  fit = NULL,
  seed = NULL
) {
    binary_positive_integer(method$n_samples, "n_samples")
    seed <- seed %||% method$control$seed
    binary_positive_integer(seed, "seed")
    settings <- NULL
    if (is.null(fit)) {
        settings <- binary_fit_control(method$control, seed)
        capacity <- settings$chains * ceiling(settings$iter_sampling / settings$thin)
        if (method$n_samples > capacity) {
            stop("`n_samples` exceeds the binary sampling budget of ", capacity, " draws.",
                call. = FALSE
            )
        }
    }
    original <- data
    fields <- c("subjid", "visit", "group", "outcome")
    columns <- unlist(vars[fields], use.names = FALSE)
    stopifnot(
        inherits(vars, "ivars"),
        is.null(vars$period),
        identical(vars$strata, vars$group),
        length(columns) == length(fields),
        !anyDuplicated(columns),
        all(columns %in% names(data))
    )
    data <- setNames(data[columns], fields)
    if (is.null(data_ice)) {
        data_ice <- data.frame(
            subjid = character(),
            visit = character(),
            strategy = character()
        )
    } else {
        ice_fields <- c("subjid", "visit", "strategy")
        data_ice <- setNames(
            data_ice[unlist(vars[ice_fields], use.names = FALSE)],
            ice_fields
        )
    }
    stopifnot(
        identical(outcome, "binary"),
        inherits(method, "bayes"),
        identical(method$covariance, "us"),
        length(method$same_cov) == 1L, is.logical(method$same_cov), !is.na(method$same_cov),
        method$prior_cov %in% c("default", "lkj"),
        is.factor(data$visit),
        is.factor(data$group),
        nlevels(data$group) == 2L,
        !anyNA(data[c("subjid", "visit", "group")]),
        is.numeric(data$outcome),
        all(na.omit(data$outcome) %in% 0:1)
    )
    ids <- unique(as.character(data$subjid))
    visits <- levels(data$visit)
    i <- match(data$subjid, ids)
    j <- as.integer(data$visit)
    arm <- data$group[match(ids, data$subjid)]
    stopifnot(
        all(data$group == arm[i]),
        !anyDuplicated(data[c("subjid", "visit")]),
        nrow(data) == length(ids) * length(visits)
    )
    Y <- matrix(
        NA_integer_,
        length(ids),
        length(visits),
        dimnames = list(ids, visits)
    )
    index <- cbind(i, j)
    Y[index] <- as.integer(data$outcome)
    baseline <- visit_covariates <- NULL
    if (length(vars$covariates)) {
        if (!all(vars$covariates %in% names(original))) {
            stop("The binary prototype expects covariate column names in `vars$covariates`.",
                call. = FALSE
            )
        }
        covariates <- original[vars$covariates]
        first_row <- match(ids, data$subjid)
        for (x in covariates) {
            if (!(is.numeric(x) || is.factor(x) || is.character(x) || is.logical(x)) ||
                !is.null(dim(x)) || anyNA(x) || (is.numeric(x) && any(!is.finite(x)))) {
                stop("Binary covariates must be finite numeric or categorical values, complete at every scheduled visit.",
                    call. = FALSE
                )
            }
        }
        model_covariates <- model.matrix(~., data = covariates)[, -1L, drop = FALSE]
        constant <- vapply(seq_len(ncol(model_covariates)), function(k) {
            all(model_covariates[, k] == model_covariates[first_row[i], k])
        }, logical(1))
        baseline <- model_covariates[first_row, constant, drop = FALSE]
        varying <- model_covariates[, !constant, drop = FALSE]
        if (ncol(varying) > 0L) {
            visit_covariates <- array(0, c(dim(Y), ncol(varying)),
                dimnames = c(dimnames(Y), list(colnames(varying)))
            )
            for (k in seq_len(ncol(varying))) {
                visit_covariates[cbind(index, k)] <- varying[, k]
            }
        }
    }

    subjects <- match(data_ice$subjid, ids)
    first <- match(data_ice$visit, visits)
    stopifnot(
        all(c("subjid", "visit", "strategy") %in% names(data_ice)),
        !anyNA(subjects),
        !anyDuplicated(subjects),
        !anyNA(first)
    )
    strategy <- setNames(rep("MAR", length(ids)), ids)
    strategy[subjects] <- binary_strategy(data_ice$strategy)
    last_on <- rep(length(visits), length(ids))
    last_on[subjects] <- first - 1L
    if (any(strategy == "LMCF" & last_on == 0L)) {
        stop("LMCF requires a scheduled visit before the ICE.", call. = FALSE)
    }
    Y_fit <- Y
    Y_fit[binary_fit_mask(Y, last_on, strategy)] <- NA_integer_
    prepared <- prepare_probit_data(
        Y_fit, as.integer(arm),
        X = if (length(vars$covariates)) binary_design(Y_fit, arm, baseline, visit_covariates),
        same_cov = method$same_cov, beta_sd = method$prior_beta_sd %||% 0
    )
    if (is.null(fit)) {
        model <- cmdstanr::cmdstan_model(cmdstanr::write_stan_file(
            probit_stan_code
        ))
        fit <- do.call(fit_probit_draws, c(list(prepared = prepared, model = model), settings))
    } else {
        stopifnot(identical(prepared, fit$prepared))
    }
    parameters <- extract_probit_draws(fit, method$n_samples, seed)
    # The fit uses numeric arm codes. Attach the corresponding treatment labels.
    parameters$metadata$arm_levels <- levels(arm)
    structure(
        list(
            data = original,
            vars = vars,
            index = index,
            Y = Y,
            baseline = baseline,
            visit_covariates = visit_covariates,
            arm = arm,
            last_on = last_on,
            strategy = strategy,
            method = method,
            fit = fit,
            diagnostics = fit$diagnostics,
            initialisation = fit$initialisation,
            fit_control = settings,
            selection_seed = seed,
            parameters = parameters
        ),
        class = "draws_binary"
    )
}

# Binary counterpart of rbmi::impute(), following impute.draws_count().
#
# draws: Binary draws object with the original data and paired parameters.
# references: Named mapping from randomized arms to reference arms.
# seed: Optional seed for conditional latent-response sampling.
# update_strategy: Optional subject ID and strategy columns for existing ICEs.
binary_impute <- function(draws, references = NULL, seed = NULL, update_strategy = NULL) {
    stopifnot(inherits(draws, "draws_binary"))
    strategy <- draws$strategy
    if (!is.null(update_strategy)) {
        fields <- unlist(draws$vars[c("subjid", "strategy")], use.names = FALSE)
        stopifnot(
            is.data.frame(update_strategy), length(update_strategy) == length(fields),
            setequal(names(update_strategy), fields)
        )
        subjects <- match(update_strategy[[draws$vars$subjid]], names(strategy))
        if (anyNA(subjects) || anyDuplicated(subjects) ||
            any(draws$last_on[subjects] == ncol(draws$Y))) {
            stop("`update_strategy` must identify distinct subjects with an existing ICE.",
                call. = FALSE
            )
        }
        strategy[subjects] <- binary_strategy(update_strategy[[draws$vars$strategy]])
        if (!identical(
            binary_fit_mask(draws$Y, draws$last_on, strategy),
            binary_fit_mask(draws$Y, draws$last_on, draws$strategy)
        )) {
            stop("This strategy update changes which observations inform the fit. Refit with the updated ICE strategies.",
                call. = FALSE
            )
        }
    }
    if (any(strategy == "LMCF" & draws$last_on == 0L)) {
        stop("LMCF requires a scheduled visit before the ICE.", call. = FALSE)
    }
    references <- binary_references(references, draws$arm, any(strategy != "MAR"))
    p <- draws$parameters
    matrices <- if (anyNA(draws$Y)) {
        impute_binary_fast(
            draws$Y, draws$arm, draws$last_on, p, references, strategy, seed,
            baseline = draws$baseline, visit_covariates = draws$visit_covariates
        )
    } else {
        rep(list(draws$Y), length(p$beta))
    }
    completed <- lapply(matrices, function(y) {
        dat <- draws$data
        dat[[draws$vars$outcome]] <- y[draws$index]
        dat
    })
    structure(
        list(
            imputations = completed, method = draws$method,
            references = references, strategy = strategy
        ),
        class = "imputation_binary"
    )
}
```

### Extract completed datasets

The prototype stores completed datasets directly. Use
`binary_extract_imputed_dfs()` to retrieve all or selected imputations.

```{r}
#| label: binary-integration-extraction
binary_extract_imputed_dfs <- function(
  imputations, index = seq_along(imputations$imputations)
) {
    stopifnot(inherits(imputations, "imputation_binary"))
    imputations$imputations[index]
}
```

### Analyse and pool

The callback receives one completed long dataset and returns the usual named
parameter list with an estimate, standard error and complete-data degrees of
freedom. Both methods fit the same unadjusted two-arm model. With
`method = "ml"`, an empty arm-by-response cell stops the fit. With
`method = "firth"`, a fit can proceed under separation when both arms are
represented. Supply the numerator and denominator treatment labels as
`treatment` and `comparator`. The odds ratio compares the named treatment
with the named comparator. See @sec-binary-firth for the rationale.

```{r}
#| label: binary-integration-analysis
# Binary endpoint callback corresponding to rbmi::ancova() in rbmi::analyse().
#
# data: One completed long dataset.
# vars: Column mapping from rbmi::set_vars().
# visit: Single endpoint visit label.
# treatment, comparator: Numerator and denominator arm labels for the odds ratio.
# method: "ml" for maximum likelihood or "firth" for mean bias reduction.
binary_logistic <- function(
  data,
  vars,
  visit,
  treatment,
  comparator,
  method = c("ml", "firth")
) {
    method <- match.arg(method)
    if (method == "firth" && !requireNamespace("brglm2", quietly = TRUE)) {
        stop(
            "Install the 'brglm2' package to use method = \"firth\".",
            call. = FALSE
        )
    }

    stopifnot(length(visit) == 1L, visit %in% levels(data[[vars$visit]]))
    stopifnot(
        is.character(treatment), length(treatment) == 1L,
        is.character(comparator), length(comparator) == 1L,
        treatment != comparator,
        setequal(c(treatment, comparator), levels(data[[vars$group]]))
    )
    at_visit <- data[[vars$visit]] == visit
    endpoint <- data.frame(
        group = data[[vars$group]][at_visit],
        outcome = data[[vars$outcome]][at_visit]
    )
    cells <- table(endpoint$group, factor(endpoint$outcome, levels = 0:1))
    if (nrow(cells) != 2L || any(rowSums(cells) == 0L)) {
        stop("Both treatment arms must be represented at the endpoint visit.")
    }
    if (method == "ml" && any(cells == 0L)) {
        stop("Week-specific logistic contrast is not estimable.")
    }

    endpoint$active <- as.integer(endpoint$group == treatment)
    fit_method <- if (method == "firth") brglm2::brglmFit else "glm.fit"
    fit_control <- if (method == "firth") list(type = "AS_mean") else list()
    fit <- glm(
        outcome ~ active,
        data = endpoint,
        family = binomial(),
        method = fit_method,
        control = fit_control
    )
    stopifnot(fit$converged)
    list(
        log_odds_ratio = list(
            est = unname(coef(fit)["active"]),
            se = sqrt(vcov(fit)["active", "active"]),
            df = df.residual(fit)
        )
    )
}

# Binary counterpart of rbmi::analyse(), using its analysis constructor.
#
# imputations: Completed datasets returned by binary_impute().
# fun: Analysis callback applied to each completed dataset.
# transform: Optional rbmi transformation specification attached to the callback.
# ...: Extra callback arguments, such as vars and visit.
binary_analyse <- function(
  imputations,
  fun = binary_logistic,
  transform = attr(fun, "transform"),
  ...
) {
    results <- lapply(binary_extract_imputed_dfs(imputations), fun, ...)
    analysis <- rbmi:::as_analysis(
        results,
        imputations$method,
        fun = fun,
        fun_name = deparse(substitute(fun)),
        transform = transform
    )
    class(analysis)[1] <- "analysis_binary"
    rbmi:::validate(analysis)
    analysis
}
```

The local adapter uses the branch's internal analysis constructor. In the
package, adding `"binary"` to its endpoint selector would assign the subclass
directly. Call `rbmi::pool()` on the result to combine log odds ratios and
their within-imputation variances. Exponentiate the pooled estimate and
interval endpoints for reporting.

## Example data analysis

Recreate the antidepressant trial's scheduled rows and translate the CIR
example's cessation assumption into ICE records. Here the last observed visit serves as
the last on-treatment visit. In a trial with recorded discontinuation dates,
derive the first affected visit from those dates. The comparison uses
`brglm2` for the Firth fit on the same completed datasets as the ML fit.

```{r}
#| label: binary-integration-trial
trial <- expand.grid(
    subjid = rownames(Ycat),
    visit = colnames(Ycat),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
trial$visit <- factor(trial$visit, levels = colnames(Ycat))
trial$group <- factor(
    treat1[match(trial$subjid, rownames(Ycat))],
    levels = 1:2,
    labels = c("Placebo", "Active")
)
trial$outcome <- as.vector(Ycat)
off <- which(last_on < ncol(Ycat))
ice <- data.frame(
    subjid = rownames(Ycat)[off],
    visit = colnames(Ycat)[last_on[off] + 1L],
    strategy = rep("CIR", length(off))
)

method <- rbmi::method_bayes(
    covariance = "us",
    same_cov = FALSE,
    n_samples = n_imp
)
vars <- rbmi::set_vars()
draw <- binary_draws(
    trial,
    ice,
    vars,
    method,
    outcome = "binary",
    fit = probit_fit,
    seed = 20261102L
)
trial_references <- c(Placebo = "Placebo", Active = "Placebo")
imp <- binary_impute(draw, references = trial_references, seed = 20261103L)
fits <- lapply(c("ml", "firth"), function(fit_method) {
    analysis <- binary_analyse(
        imp,
        binary_logistic,
        vars = vars,
        visit = "week8",
        treatment = "Active",
        comparator = "Placebo",
        method = fit_method
    )
    contrast <- rbmi::pool(analysis)$pars$log_odds_ratio
    exp(c(contrast$est, contrast$ci))
})
comparison <- data.frame(
    Method = c("Maximum likelihood", "Firth"),
    Odds_ratio = vapply(fits, function(odds) odds[1], numeric(1)),
    Lower_95 = vapply(fits, function(odds) odds[2], numeric(1)),
    Upper_95 = vapply(fits, function(odds) odds[3], numeric(1))
)
# Check that the full workflow reproduces the standalone CIR imputations.
stopifnot(
    all(vapply(
        seq_len(n_imp),
        function(m) {
            identical(
                imp$imputations[[m]]$outcome,
                as.vector(cir_completed[[m]])
            )
        },
        logical(1)
    ))
)
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 3)
```

Both fits use the same `r length(imp$imputations)` completed datasets and
the same Barnard–Rubin pooling. The pooled Week 8 active-versus-placebo odds
ratios under CIR are similar. The completed outcomes match the standalone
imputation example exactly.

### Factor order regression check

Reverse the treatment levels and reorder the posterior mean and covariance
blocks to match. Reuse the same parameter draws, reference mapping, and
Active-versus-Placebo contrast. With the same imputation seed, the completed
outcomes and pooled log odds ratio, including its interval, should agree exactly.

```{r}
#| label: binary-reference-order-check
reversed_draw <- draw
arm_order <- rev(seq_along(levels(draw$arm)))
reversed_levels <- levels(draw$arm)[arm_order]
reversed_draw$arm <- factor(draw$arm, levels = reversed_levels)
reversed_draw$data[[vars$group]] <- factor(trial$group, levels = reversed_levels)
reversed_draw$parameters$metadata$arm_levels <- reversed_levels
beta_order <- as.vector(matrix(seq_len(2L * ncol(draw$Y)), ncol = 2)[, arm_order])
reversed_draw$parameters$beta <- lapply(draw$parameters$beta, `[`, beta_order)
reversed_draw$parameters$sigma <- lapply(draw$parameters$sigma, `[`, arm_order)
reversed_imp <- binary_impute(reversed_draw, references = trial_references, seed = 20261103L)

week8_contrast <- function(imputations, fit_method, vars = rbmi::set_vars()) {
    rbmi::pool(binary_analyse(
        imputations,
        binary_logistic,
        vars = vars,
        visit = "week8",
        treatment = "Active",
        comparator = "Placebo",
        method = fit_method
    ))$pars$log_odds_ratio
}
stopifnot(identical(
    lapply(imp$imputations, `[[`, vars$outcome),
    lapply(reversed_imp$imputations, `[[`, vars$outcome)
))
for (fit_method in c("ml", "firth")) {
    stopifnot(identical(
        week8_contrast(imp, fit_method),
        week8_contrast(reversed_imp, fit_method)
    ))
}
```

### Baseline-adjusted imputation

Use baseline HAMD17 in the imputation model, centered at the patient-level
mean and measured in five-point units. Each visit has its own baseline
slope. The adjusted model is fitted afresh with a latent coefficient prior
standard deviation of 2. The Week 8 analysis fits the same treatment-only logistic
model, so its odds ratio has the same marginal interpretation as in the
unadjusted imputation example.

```{r}
#| label: binary-covariate-trial
baseline_hamd <- with(antidepressant, basval[match(rownames(Ycat), PATIENT)])
stopifnot(all(is.finite(baseline_hamd)))
trial$baseline_hamd <- (baseline_hamd[match(trial$subjid, rownames(Ycat))] -
    mean(baseline_hamd)) / 5
adjusted_vars <- rbmi::set_vars(covariates = "baseline_hamd")
adjusted_draw <- binary_draws(
    trial, ice, adjusted_vars,
    method_bayes_binary(same_cov = FALSE, n_samples = n_imp, prior_beta_sd = 2),
    seed = 20261104L
)
adjusted_imp <- binary_impute(
    adjusted_draw,
    references = trial_references, seed = 20261103L
)
stopifnot(all(vapply(adjusted_imp$imputations, function(completed) {
    observed <- !is.na(trial$outcome)
    identical(completed$outcome[observed], trial$outcome[observed]) &&
        !anyNA(completed$outcome) &&
        identical(completed$baseline_hamd, trial$baseline_hamd)
}, logical(1))))
adjusted_contrasts <- lapply(c("ml", "firth"), function(fit_method) {
    week8_contrast(adjusted_imp, fit_method, vars = adjusted_vars)
})
knitr::kable(data.frame(
    Method = c("Maximum likelihood", "Firth"),
    Odds_ratio = vapply(adjusted_contrasts, function(x) exp(x$est), numeric(1)),
    Lower_95 = vapply(adjusted_contrasts, function(x) exp(x$ci[1]), numeric(1)),
    Upper_95 = vapply(adjusted_contrasts, function(x) exp(x$ci[2]), numeric(1))
), digits = 3)
```

The following check gives two patients the same arm, missingness pattern and
ICE time, with opposite baseline values. The coefficients make their
pre-ICE randomized-arm means identical. After the ICE, CIR uses different
reference-arm increments for the two patients. A separate treatment setting
in the design matrix verifies that the coefficient order matches the
imputer's calculations. Reversing the arm levels and their intercept blocks
leaves the covariate slopes and completed outcomes unchanged.

```{r}
#| label: binary-covariate-check
check_y <- matrix(NA_integer_, 2, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("early", "late")))
check_arm <- factor(rep("Active", 2), levels = c("Placebo", "Active"))
check_baseline <- matrix(c(-1, 1), ncol = 1, dimnames = list(NULL, "baseline"))
check_beta <- c(5, -5, 10, 20, 0, 30)
check_parameters <- list(
    beta = list(check_beta), sigma = list(list(diag(2))),
    metadata = list(arm_levels = levels(check_arm))
)
for (arm_name in levels(check_arm)) {
    check_design <- binary_design(
        check_y, factor(rep(arm_name, 2), levels = levels(check_arm)), check_baseline
    )
    check_means <- matrix(matrix(check_design, nrow = 4) %*% check_beta, 2, 2)
    intercept <- if (arm_name == "Placebo") c(5, -5) else c(10, 20)
    expected <- rep(1, 2) %o% intercept + check_baseline %*% rbind(c(0, 30))
    stopifnot(identical(check_means, expected))
}
check_completed <- impute_binary_fast(
    check_y, check_arm, c(1L, 1L), check_parameters, trial_references,
    rep("CIR", 2),
    seed = 42L, baseline = check_baseline
)[[1]]
stopifnot(identical(unname(check_completed), cbind(c(1L, 1L), c(0L, 1L))))
check_reversed_levels <- rev(levels(check_arm))
check_parameters$metadata$arm_levels <- check_reversed_levels
check_parameters$beta[[1]] <- check_beta[c(3L, 4L, 1L, 2L, 5L, 6L)]
stopifnot(identical(check_completed, impute_binary_fast(
    check_y, factor(check_arm, levels = check_reversed_levels), c(1L, 1L),
    check_parameters, trial_references, rep("CIR", 2),
    seed = 42L, baseline = check_baseline
)[[1]]))
```

### Separation example

To illustrate separation, take a copy of the first completed dataset and set
the placebo responses at Week 8 to zero. This modified dataset illustrates the
failure mode on a single fit.

```{r}
#| label: binary-firth-separation
separated <- imp$imputations[[1]]
separated$outcome[
    separated$visit == "week8" & separated$group == "Placebo"
] <- 0L
ml_fit <- tryCatch(
    binary_logistic(separated, vars,
        visit = "week8", treatment = "Active",
        comparator = "Placebo", method = "ml"
    ),
    error = identity
)
firth_fit <- binary_logistic(
    separated,
    vars,
    visit = "week8",
    treatment = "Active",
    comparator = "Placebo",
    method = "firth"
)$log_odds_ratio
stopifnot(
    inherits(ml_fit, "error"),
    is.finite(firth_fit$est),
    is.finite(firth_fit$se)
)
```

With `method = "ml"`, `binary_logistic()` stops because the
active-versus-placebo maximum likelihood estimate is infinite. With
`method = "firth"`, it returns a finite odds ratio
of `r sprintf("%.2f", exp(firth_fit$est))` and a log odds ratio standard error
of `r sprintf("%.2f", firth_fit$se)`.

### Sparse and unobserved cells

Start with a scheduled two-visit dataset. In the sparse case, every observed
Active response at Week 1 is zero and one is missing. In the empty-cell case,
all Week 1 Active responses are missing. Both cases also have a missing
Week 8 response. Use a prior standard deviation of 1 on the latent scale for
these fixtures.

```{r}
#| label: binary-sparse-cell-check
sparse_trial <- expand.grid(subjid = seq_len(24L), visit = c("week1", "week8"))
sparse_trial$group <- factor(
    ifelse(sparse_trial$subjid <= 12L, "Placebo", "Active"),
    levels = c("Placebo", "Active")
)
sparse_trial$outcome <- sparse_trial$subjid %% 2L
early_active <- with(sparse_trial, visit == "week1" & group == "Active")
sparse_trial$outcome[early_active] <- 0L
sparse_trial$outcome[which(early_active)[1L]] <- NA_integer_
sparse_trial$outcome[with(sparse_trial, visit == "week8" & subjid == 24L)] <- NA_integer_
sparse_trial$outcome[with(sparse_trial, visit == "week8" & subjid == 14L)] <- NA_integer_
empty_trial <- sparse_trial
empty_trial$outcome[early_active] <- NA_integer_

sparse_method <- method_bayes_binary(
    same_cov = TRUE, n_samples = 30L, prior_beta_sd = 1,
    control = rbmi::control_bayes(
        warmup = 500L, chains = 2L, thin = 2L, seed = 20261102L, iter_sampling = 600L
    )
)
check_sparse_workflow <- function(data, data_ice = NULL, method = sparse_method) {
    flat_method <- method
    flat_method$prior_beta_sd <- 0
    flat_error <- tryCatch(
        binary_draws(data, data_ice, vars = vars, method = flat_method),
        error = identity
    )
    stopifnot(
        inherits(flat_error, "error"),
        grepl("Flat priors require both outcomes", conditionMessage(flat_error), fixed = TRUE)
    )

    draws <- binary_draws(data, data_ice, vars = vars, method = method)
    completed <- binary_impute(draws, references = trial_references, seed = 20261103L)
    observed <- !is.na(data$outcome)
    stopifnot(
        length(draws$parameters$sigma[[1]]) == if (method$same_cov) 1L else 2L,
        posterior::nchains(draws$fit$fit$draws("beta")) == method$control$chains,
        posterior::niterations(draws$fit$fit$draws("beta")) == 300L,
        length(draws$initialisation) == method$control$chains,
        !is.null(draws$diagnostics),
        draws$fit$prepared$data$beta_sd == method$prior_beta_sd,
        draws$fit_control$seed == method$control$seed,
        length(completed$imputations) == method$n_samples,
        all(vapply(completed$imputations, function(dat) {
            all(dat$outcome %in% 0:1) &&
                identical(dat$outcome[observed], data$outcome[observed])
        }, logical(1)))
    )
    pooled <- week8_contrast(completed, "firth")
    stopifnot(all(is.finite(c(pooled$est, pooled$ci))), length(pooled$ci) == 2L)
    list(draws = draws, pooled = pooled)
}

sparse_ice <- data.frame(
    subjid = c(13L, 24L, 14L), visit = c("week8", "week1", "week8"),
    strategy = c("CIR", "CIR", "MAR")
)
oversized_method <- sparse_method
oversized_method$n_samples <- 601L
budget_error <- tryCatch(
    binary_draws(sparse_trial, sparse_ice, vars, oversized_method),
    error = identity
)
stopifnot(
    inherits(budget_error, "error"),
    grepl("exceeds the binary sampling budget", conditionMessage(budget_error), fixed = TRUE)
)
sparse_check <- check_sparse_workflow(sparse_trial, sparse_ice)
empty_method <- sparse_method
empty_method$same_cov <- FALSE
empty_check <- check_sparse_workflow(empty_trial, method = empty_method)

set.seed(20261103L)
implicit_seed_imp <- binary_impute(sparse_check$draws, references = trial_references)
previous_rng <- .Random.seed
stopifnot(identical(implicit_seed_imp, binary_impute(
    sparse_check$draws,
    references = trial_references, seed = 20261103L
)))
invisible(binary_impute(sparse_check$draws, references = trial_references))
stopifnot(!identical(previous_rng, .Random.seed))
```

### Strategy sensitivity checks

Reuse the sparse example's fit. Subject 13 has a missing first outcome and an
observed Week 8 response at the ICE. Subject 24 has an ICE at the first
scheduled visit. Both start with CIR, so their observed responses from the
ICE onward were masked. Subject 14 has an ICE at Week 8 and a missing response
there, so switching that subject from MAR to CIR leaves the fit unchanged.

```{r}
#| label: binary-strategy-check
strategy_draws <- sparse_check$draws
for (strategy_name in c("J2R", "CR", "CIR", "LMCF")) {
    update <- data.frame(subjid = 13L, strategy = strategy_name)
    if (strategy_name != "LMCF") {
        update <- rbind(update, data.frame(subjid = 24L, strategy = strategy_name))
    }
    strategy_imp <- binary_impute(
        strategy_draws,
        references = trial_references, update_strategy = update
    )
    observed <- !is.na(sparse_trial$outcome)
    stopifnot(
        strategy_imp$strategy[["13"]] == if (strategy_name == "J2R") "JR" else strategy_name,
        all(vapply(strategy_imp$imputations, function(dat) {
            all(dat$outcome %in% 0:1) &&
                identical(dat$outcome[observed], sparse_trial$outcome[observed])
        }, logical(1))),
        all(is.finite(week8_contrast(strategy_imp, "firth")$ci))
    )
}
same_fit <- binary_impute(
    strategy_draws,
    references = trial_references,
    update_strategy = data.frame(subjid = 14L, strategy = "CIR")
)
stopifnot(same_fit$strategy[["14"]] == "CIR", strategy_draws$strategy[["14"]] == "MAR")
invalid_mar <- tryCatch(binary_impute(
    strategy_draws,
    references = trial_references,
    update_strategy = data.frame(subjid = 13L, strategy = "MAR")
), error = identity)
stopifnot(
    inherits(invalid_mar, "error"),
    grepl("Refit with the updated ICE strategies", conditionMessage(invalid_mar), fixed = TRUE)
)
invalid_lmcf <- tryCatch(binary_impute(
    strategy_draws,
    references = trial_references,
    update_strategy = data.frame(subjid = 24L, strategy = "LMCF")
), error = identity)
stopifnot(
    inherits(invalid_lmcf, "error"),
    grepl("scheduled visit before the ICE", conditionMessage(invalid_lmcf), fixed = TRUE)
)

# Three visits with distinct randomized and reference pre-ICE correlations.
fixture_means <- cbind(c(0, 1, 3), c(2, 4, 5))
fixture_cov <- list(
    matrix(c(1, .2, .1, .2, 1, .3, .1, .3, 1), 3),
    matrix(c(1, .5, 0, .5, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1), 3)
)
targets <- lapply(c("MAR", "JR", "CR", "CIR", "LMCF"), function(strategy_name) {
    binary_distribution(fixture_means, fixture_cov, 2L, 1L, 2L, strategy_name)
})
conditional_moments <- function(Sigma) {
    cross <- Sigma[3, 1:2, drop = FALSE]
    B <- cross %*% solve(Sigma[1:2, 1:2])
    c(B, Sigma[3, 3] - B %*% t(cross))
}
stopifnot(
    identical(lapply(targets, `[[`, "mu"), list(
        c(2, 4, 5), c(2, 4, 3), c(0, 1, 3), c(2, 4, 6), c(2, 4, 4)
    )),
```
